On BrowseComp-Plus (a deep-research quiz where the agent must search and answer hard questions), same Qwen3.6-27B, 32K context limit, versus the strongest outside summary-compaction baseline (an outside loop that shortens the transcript for the model):

Editable-context run: 59.4% 11.4% relative above that summary baseline 21.5% fewer prefix-reuse floating-point operations (FLOPs: how much compute the run burned, including recompute after mid-context edits)

Shao et al. call this a Context Language Model (CLM). The text the model can see this turn is an editable file. The model may rewrite it with ordinary shell commands, and each edit syncs into the next turn. Context management moves out of the harness (the outside loop that decides what stays in working memory) and into model behavior.

In their traces the model opens that file, invents a notes role mid-history, and strips stale search dumps itself. No outside summary policy choosing what survives.

Same pattern on a 12-hour repository optimization suite (EdgeBench-10): 5% higher scores with 59% fewer FLOPs against that outside-summary baseline (Qwen: 44.6 at 179 PF vs summary 42.3 at 437 PF).

If you ship long-running agents, measure whether your outside trim and summarize policy is the bottleneck, versus letting the model rewrite its own working memory.

What I still want measured is how often a free context edit deletes the one fact the next turn needed, and whether teams can audit that deletion before it compounds.
